en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the thirty-sixth year had arrived, Yudhiṣṭhira, the joy of the Kurus, beheld adverse omens. Harsh winds, accompanied by thunderclaps, blew, raining down gravel.
The birds moved in counter-clockwise circles;
the great rivers flowed backward, and the quarters of the sky were shrouded in mist.
Meteors, raining down glowing embers, fell from the heavens to the earth.

O King, at sunrise, the orb of the sun was always seen completely shrouded by dust, its rays extinguished, appearing like a headless trunk; and dreadful halos were observed around both the moon and the sun.

"O King, these and many other portents foreboding fear— such as those appearing in three colors, dark and rough at their ends, and possessing an ashy-red luster— are seen day after day, causing agitation in the heart."

While the Lord of the world desired to ascend to heaven, these were seen: by whose grace this Dharma exists in the Kali age just as it did in the Kṛta age; and the highly fortunate Pāṇḍavas, who are endowed with glory and are sinless.

Then, after some time had passed, Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of the Kurus, heard that a slaughter had been committed with the maces of the Vṛṣṇi host. And having heard that Vāsudeva and Rāma had departed [from this world], the Pāṇḍava [was deeply moved].

Having gathered together, he said to his brothers, "What shall we do? Upon hearing that the Vṛṣṇis had perished, having been overcome by the power of the Brahman's staff, the Pāṇḍavas met one another and were deeply distressed.
The heroes could not believe in the destruction of Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, which was like the drying up of the ocean;
having heard of the *mausala* [incident], they were filled with pain and grief.
Dejected and with their resolutions shattered, the Pāṇḍavas sat down together.
Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, how were the Andhakas destroyed along with the Vṛṣṇis?"
While Vāsudeva was looking on, the Bhojas and the great chariot-warriors likewise [beheld him]. Having honored and bowed down to you, I ask this of you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, in the thirty-sixth year from that time, a great calamity befell the Vṛṣṇis;
impelled by Time, they struck one another with clubs.
Janamejaya said:
"By whom were those heroes cursed that the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas went to their destruction, as did the Bhojas, O best of the twice-born? Tell me this in detail.
Vaiśampāyana said:
The heroes, headed by Sāraṇa, beheld Viśvāmitra, Kaṇva, and Nārada, whose wealth is asceticism, arrived at Dvārakā. Placing Sāmba at their head, they adorned him like a woman.
Afflicted by the rod of fate, they approached and said:
"O sages, please consider well: this woman belongs to Babhru of immeasurable splendor, who desires a son; what will she bring forth?"
O King, having been addressed thus, those sages, who had been provoked by that deception, replied to them; hear what they said, O lord of men:
"For the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, there shall be a terrible iron club."
This Samba, the heir of Vāsudeva,
shall beget one by whom you— so wicked, cruel, and filled with wrath—
shall utterly destroy your entire lineage, with the sole exception of Rāma and Janārdana.
"The illustrious Halāyudha will go to the ocean after casting off his body;
old age will break down the high-souled Kṛṣṇa as he lies upon the earth.
Thus they spoke, O King, having been deceived by those evil-minded ones.
Then the sages, their eyes red with anger, looked at one another;
having spoken thus, those sages then approached Keśava.
Then Madhusūdana, having heard this from the Vṛṣṇis, spoke.
"Knowing the end and possessed of wisdom, he must become such [as you have described].
Having spoken thus to them, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Lord of the universe, entered his home again; that Master did not wish to make the decree of destiny otherwise.
Then, when the next day had dawned, Sāmba indeed gave birth to that pestle (*musala*) by which the men of the Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka clans were reduced to ashes—
a great weapon resembling a servant of Yama, destined for the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
They reported to the king that terrible thing born of the curse which had been produced; then the king, appearing dejected, had it ground into a fine powder,
and by the king's command, his men cast it into the ocean.
O King, those men also cast that powder into the ocean;
once prepared by them, the powder produced waves in the great sea.
And by the command of Āhuka,
Janārdana, Rāma, and the high-souled Babhru, he caused this proclamation to be made throughout the city:
"From this day forward, in all the houses of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas here..."
"16,002.018c No *surāsava* (liquor) shall be prepared by any of the city-dwellers. 16,002.019a And if any man anywhere should secretly prepare such a drink for us,
16,002.019c he, having done so himself, shall be impaled alive upon a stake along with his kinsmen."
Then, out of fear of the king, all the people established a restraint at that time,
having received the command and decree of that high-souled monarch.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas were thus striving,
Time (Kāla) constantly wandered through the houses of them all—
a man who was formidable, misshapen, shaven-headed, and dark-brown in hue.
Karaṭa is a shaven-headed man with dark-brown eyes;
he possesses a great banner in his assembly, wears a hibiscus flower as an ornament,
rides upon a chameleon, and is adorned with the feathers of a crow.

Having searched the houses of the Vṛṣṇis, he was not seen anywhere again. The great archers struck him with hundreds of thousands of arrows, yet he could not be pierced, for he was then the cause of the destruction of all beings.
Day after day, fierce and hair-raising great winds arose in great numbers for the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas;
likewise, the streets swarmed with rats and the water-jars were shattered.
The hair and nails of those who sleep are eaten by mice at night;
the sarika birds shriek "cī-cī-kū-cī" within the dwellings of the Vṛṣṇis,
and that sound does not cease, continuing indeed day and night.
O Bhārata, imitating the cries of owls as well as those of cranes, goats likewise mimicked the howling of jackals;
and pale birds with red feet, impelled by Time, appeared.
At that time, pigeons wandered through the houses of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas;
donkeys were born from cows, and young camels from mules; cats were born from bitches, and mice from mongooses.
At that time, the Vṛṣṇis committed sins without feeling shame;
they even showed hatred toward the Brāhmaṇas, as well as toward the ancestors and the gods.
They also held their elders in contempt, yet they did not treat Rāma and Janārdana with such disregard.
Husbands were unfaithful to their wives, and likewise wives to their husbands.
The blazing fire,
emitting flames of blue, red, and madder-brown, flickered in various directions.

In that city, the sun was constantly seen by men rising and setting, repeatedly surrounded by headless trunks (kabandhas). O Bhārata, when food had been prepared and thoroughly refined in the kitchens, [the same occurred].
O lord of men, as the [funeral] pyre was being brought forward, worms were seen;
and while auspicious days were being proclaimed and the high-souled ones were chanting prayers,
the piercing howls of dogs were heard on all sides.
The sounds of people running were heard, yet no one was seen;
and they all beheld the stars being struck again and again by the planets, but they could not perceive it at all in relation to themselves.
As the Pāñcajanya conch resounded within the dwellings of the Vṛṣ� donis and Andhakas,
donkeys with harsh voices brayed from all sides.
Observing this, Hṛṣīkeśa perceived that the turn of time had arrived.
Seeing that [eclipse] on the thirteenth day, at the new moon, he spoke this:
"This fourteenth and fifteenth day has been made so again by Rāhu;
and now, in the battle of Bhārata, it has arrived for our destruction."
Reflecting upon that time and considering it carefully, Janārdana,
the slayer of Keśin, realized that the thirty-sixth year had indeed arrived. Gāndhārī, whose kinsmen had been slain, was consumed by the grief for her son.
"That which she, in her distress, uttered as a prophecy has now come to pass.
Yudhiṣṭhira spoke of this very thing when he saw those most terrible portents in the past, before the armies were arrayed."
"Neither from the mere giving of meritorious gifts, nor from the delusion of tranquility alone,
nor from the performance of meritorious deeds, would there be any other higher good.
Having said this, Vāsudeva, desiring that very truth, [proceeded].
Then, O subduer of enemies, he commanded a pilgrimage to the sacred fords (tīrthayātrā).
At the command of Keśava, men proclaimed there:
"O bulls among men, you must undertake a pilgrimage to the ocean."
Vaiśampāyana said:
A black woman with white teeth, laughing as she enters at night,
runs through Dvārakā in dreams, stealing from the women.
In the fire-sanctuaries, in the centers of the dwellings, and within the houses,
terrifying vultures devoured the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas in their dreams, uttering fearsome and discordant shrieks.
Likewise, those with two heads, the fierce ones, and those with four arms are born from the wombs of women, as are Rākṣasas and Guhyakas. So too are ornaments, umbrellas, banners, and armor.
They were seen being carried away by most terrifying *rākṣasas*.
Then, that iron wheel of Kṛṣṇa, given by Agni and with a hub like a thunderbolt, soared toward the sky while the Vṛṣṇis looked on.
While Dāruka looked on, they brought forth a yoked, divine chariot, radiant as the sun; those horses moved across the surface of the ocean.
The four preeminent steeds, swift as thought— Tāla and Suparṇa, those two great banners—
were highly honored by Rāma and Janārdana.
Day and night, the Apsarases cried out loudly,
"Go on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords!"—
for those whose enjoyments were spread wide by the sight, touch, and affection of the Blessed One.

For the purpose of entering heaven, they ascended to the celestial realm in their celestial chariots (*vimāna*). Then those great car-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, bulls among men, desiring to depart, wished to undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords (*tīrthayātrā*) together with their harems.
Then the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis prepared abundant food, snacks,
and drinks of many kinds, including various liquors and meats in great quantities. Then, addicted to these spirits, they went out from the city.
Accompanied by chariots, horses, and elephants, those illustrious and fiercely radiant ones then dwelt at Prabhāsa, each according to his designated place and his own home; there,
the Yādavas, together with their wives, enjoyed an abundance of food and drink.

Then, having learned that they had settled at the edge of the ocean, Uddhava, the knower of yoga and expert in worldly affairs, took leave of those heroes and departed. As that high-souled one was setting out, [the others] saluted him with palms joined in reverence.
Knowing the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis was at hand, Hari did not wish to prevent it.
Then those great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka clans, overcome by time,
beheld Uddhava departing, pervading heaven and earth with his splendor.
Whatever food was prepared for the sake of those high-souled brahmins,
they gave it to the monkeys, infused with the fragrance of wine.
Then, the place resounded with hundreds of musical instruments and was crowded with actors and dancers.
A great drinking bout took place at Prabhāsa among those of fierce energy.
In the presence of Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, together with Kṛtavarman,
as well as Yuyudhāna, Gada, and Babhru, drank [the wine].
Then, in the midst of the assembly, Yuyudhāna, intoxicated with pride,
spoke to Kṛtavarman, laughing at him and treating him with contempt:
"What man who considers himself a kṣatriya would slay those who are asleep, as if they were already dead?"
"O Hārdikya, the Yādavas do not forgive that which was done by you;
nor does Hārdikya forgive that which he spoke then in his wrath. When Yuyudhāna had said this, [Kṛṣṇa] honored those words.
Pradyumna, the best of chariot-warriors, having disregarded the son of Hṛdika,
then became exceedingly enraged; and Kṛtavarman spoke to him,
pointing with his left hand as if in contempt.
"How was Bhūriśravas, whose arm had been severed in battle and who had entered the vow of fasting (*prāya*), struck down by you,
a hero, with such a cruel slaughter?
Having heard these words of his, Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes, [replied].
The wrathful one cast a sidelong glance with a look full of anger. Then Sātyaki reminded Madhusūdana of that story concerning the Syamantaka jewel which had belonged to Satrājit.
Having heard that, Satyabhāmā, filled with rage and inciting Janārdana, went then weeping to Keśava’s lap. Then Sātyaki, rising up in anger, spoke these words:
"Of the five sons of Draupadī, of Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin—
of these I shall follow the path; I swear this by the truth—
that they were slain while sleeping by this evil-souled man during the night attack."

"O slender-waisted one, today his life and his fame have come to an end through the evil Kṛtavarman, who was aided by the son of Droṇa. Having said this, [he struck him] with a sword in the presence of Keśava.
Rushing forward in a rage, he severed the head of Kṛtavarman;
then Hṛṣīkeśa ran toward Yuyudhāna, who was likewise slaughtering others on all sides, in order to restrain him.
Then, all of them, impelled by the turn of time, united as one;
O great king, the Bhojas and Andhakas surrounded the descendant of Śini.
Seeing them rushing forward swiftly and filled with rage, Janārdana—
The one of great splendor did not become angry, knowing the turning of time. But they, intoxicated by drink and impelled by fury,
then struck Yuyudhāna with their leftover vessels.
While the grandson of Śini was being struck down, the son of Rukmiṇī became enraged;
rushing into that interval, he sought to liberate the son of Śini.
Satyaki then engaged with the Bhojas, while [the others] engaged with the Andhakas.
Those two heroes, exerting themselves and endowed with the strength of their arms,
were both slain there due to the great number [of the enemy], even as Kṛṣṇa looked on.
Seeing Śaineya slain, as well as his own son, the joy of the Yadus—
Then Keśava, out of anger, seized a handful of *erakā* grass;
it became a terrible iron club, like a thunderbolt.
With that, Kṛṣṇa struck those who stood before him.
Then the Andhakas, the Bhojas, the Śaineyas, and the Vṛṣṇis,
impelled by Time, slaughtered one another in the clamor of battle with clubs,
O King; for whoever among them seized an *eraka* grass in his rage, [it became a club].
O King, O Lord, she then appeared like one made of adamant;
even a blade of grass was seen there as having become a mace.
Know this, O Ruler of the Earth, that everything was brought about by the Brahma-staff.
O King, whatever blade of grass they repeatedly brandished and hurled,
that was then seen as a firm mace made of adamant; thus,
O Bhārata, son slew father and father slew son.
Intoxicated, they rushed about, striking one another;
like moths into a fire, those Kukurās and Andhakas fell down. As they were being slaughtered, not a single one had the thought of fleeing.
But seeing him, the mighty-armed Madhusūdana, knowing the turn of time, stood leaning upon his mace.
And Mādhava beheld Sāmba slain, as well as Cārudeṣṇa.
Seeing Pradyumna and Aniruddha, O Bhārata, he then became enraged;
and beholding Gada lying there, filled with intense fury,
the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and the mace then made an end of them all.
As he was thus slaughtering [the enemy], the immensely energetic Babhru, the conqueror of hostile cities, and Dāruka spoke to the descendant of Daśārha; hear what they said:
"O Blessed One, O Acyuta, almost everything has been destroyed by you."
"Seek out the path of Rāma; let us go there where he is.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Dāruka and Keśava departed.
And Babhru, as he was falling at Rāma’s feet,
then beheld Rāma of infinite prowess,
standing alone beneath a tree, lost in thought.
Then, having approached him, the high-souled Kṛṣṇa commanded Dāruka:
"Go quickly to the Kurus and [inform them] of this great matter."
"Tell Pārtha of the slaughter of the Yādavas;
then Arjuna shall quickly come here upon hearing that the Yādavas have perished through the curse of a Brahmin."
Having been addressed thus, Dāruka then departed for the Kurus by chariot, his mind distraught. After Dāruka had gone, Keśava then—
Seeing Babhru nearby, he spoke these words:
"Go quickly and protect the women; otherwise, these bandits might harm them out of greed for wealth."
Instructed by Keśava, he set out,
though intoxicated with pride and tormented by the slaughter of his kinsmen;
indeed, as he was departing in the presence of Keśava—
You suddenly slew the solitary Babhru as he was hurrying away,
though he had been cursed by a Brahmin;
indeed, you [wielded] the hunter’s club released from its concealment.
Then, seeing that Babhru had been slain,
Kṛṣṇa spoke these words to his elder brother:
"O Rāma, wait for me right here."
"Until women are under the control of their kinsmen," [he said].
Then, having entered the city of Dvāravatī,
Janārdana spoke these words to his father:
"May you protect all our women while awaiting the arrival of Dhanañjaya;
as Rāma protected me at the edge of the forest."
"I remain here today; I shall meet with him.
I have witnessed this destruction of the Yadus, as well as that of the kings who were formerly the bulls among the Kurus."
"I am not able to look upon this city of the Yādavas today without the Yadus;
know this from me, for I shall practice ascetic penance."
"Having gone to the forest together with Rāma,"—
having spoken thus and touched his feet with his head, Kṛṣṇa departed in haste.
Then a great roar arose from that city, including its women and children;
then Keśava, turning back, spoke:
Hearing the cries of the women,
Savyasācin will come to this city;
that foremost of men will liberate you from your sorrows.
16,005.011c Then, having gone there, Keśava beheld him;
Rāma was standing alone in a secluded part of the forest.
16,005.012a Then he saw that [Rāma] who was absorbed in yoga;
Then, seeing a great white elephant emerging from his mouth, that high-souled one proceeded toward the great ocean while being watched by him.
The high-souled Śveta also went toward the great ocean, gazing upon it;
he was thousand-headed and possessed a body as vast as a mountain range.
Having abandoned that body of his, Raktānana was seen entering the edge of the ocean,
and the ocean duly received him.
The divine Nāgas and sacred rivers,
Karkoṭaka, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Pṛthuśravas, Varuṇa, and Kuñjara; 16,005.014a.
Miśrī, Śaṅkha, Kumuda, and Puṇḍarīka;
likewise the high-souled Nāga Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
Hrāda, Krātha, Śitikaṇṭha, and Agratejas.
Likewise, O King, there were the two Nāgas Cakramanda and Tiṣaṇḍa, as well as Durmukha, the best of Nāgas, and Ambarīṣa;
and Varuṇa himself was also present, O King.
They went out to meet him and greeted him with a welcome;
they honored him with the rites of offering water for the hands and feet.
Having assembled there, they appeared like gods among men.
Rejoicing and worshipping the primordial god Saṃkarṣaṇa, the upholder of the earth and the one of pure intellect,
Vāsudeva then [departed] when his brother had gone.
Knowing all destinies and possessing divine vision,
he wandered through the empty forest reflecting; then,
that one of supreme splendor lay down upon the ground.
For everything he had previously known was already understood by him when he was formerly addressed by Gāndhārī,
and when he was smeared with the remnants of the milk-rice by Durvāsas.
And Kṛṣṇa also recalled what had been said:
that he had taken away the strength of virtuous women of noble lineage, of cows, and of the best of the twice-born, for the sake of dharma.
The source of the gods, the granter of boons, the divine Brahmā,
known as Govinda, Vāsudeva, and eternal— he,
reflecting upon the destruction of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis;
The high-souled one then perceived that the time for his departure had come;
he then performed the withdrawal of his senses.
And just as for the sake of maintaining the stability of the world,
for the sake of fulfilling the words of Durvāsas,
and for the sake of dispelling the doubt of the god...
He who knows the truth of all objects desired a sign; then Kṛṣṇa, having restrained his senses, speech, and mind, lay down, having entered into great yoga.
Then,
at that moment, a fierce hunter, desiring game,
arrived at that place; he saw Keśava lying there, absorbed in yoga.
Suspecting him to be a deer, the hunter, acting with haste,
pierced him in the sole of his foot with an arrow;
and he approached him from all sides, desiring to seize him.
Drawing his arrow, Jarā pierced the sleeping Kṛṣṇa in the foot, mistaking him for a deer.
Then he beheld a man absorbed in yoga.
Thinking himself an offender against him, the hunter, who wore yellow garments and possessed many arms,
took his feet with his head in a state of great distress.
Then that Great-Souled One,
ascending and pervading heaven and earth with his splendor,
comforted him out of remorse for his actions and his birth.
Having seen the Lord of infinite prowess thus, Kṛṣṇa was cast off from his body by the gods and led to heaven; there he was honored by the hosts of sages.
Then Kṛṣṇa comforted him; and as he ascended, pervading the worlds with his own splendor,
he was suddenly perceived through the application of yoga.
Then Vāsava, the two Aśvins,
the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Viśvedevas,
as well as the sages and the Siddhas, went forth to meet him who had reached heaven.
The leaders of the Gandharvas, together with the Apsarases,
and all the Uragas as well,
praised him there along with the most excellent Apsarases.
Then, O King, the Blessed One, Nārāyaṇa— of fierce splendor, the source of all, and imperishable—
the teacher of yoga, pervaded heaven and earth with his majesty.
The high-souled one attained his own immeasurable station.
Then, O King, Kṛṣṇa was joined by the gods, the ṛṣis, and the cāraṇas.
Then Madhusūdana was joined by all those gods, sages, and Cāraṇas,
as well as by the foremost Gandharvas and the most excellent Apsarases.
Being worshipped by the Siddhas and Sādhyas who bowed down before him,
O King, those gods indeed rejoiced and honored the Lord with words, O best of sages.
Being approached by Śiva, Brahmā, and the other world-protectors, and being praised by hosts of gods and siddhas,
the gandharvas also stood nearby offering hymns of praise.
And Puruhūta greeted him with affection:
"Salutations, salutations to you, O Blessed One, wielder of the Śārṅga bow! You have appeared upon the earth for the preservation of Dharma."
Having slain all the enemies of the gods, beginning with the one named Kaṃsa,
the earth was established for the sake of the descendants of Bharata;
[he attained] a divine, undecaying, and immeasurable station.
Difficult to comprehend, yet accessible through the scriptures, supreme—
go forth, O Lord, and protect those who have come to you in distress;
being born in every aeon in your own form.
Having spoken thus, the host of gods followed him and,
endowed with splendor, rained down a shower of flowers;
for that speech was present there in embodied form.
O King, enter into the center of the sun;
this distinguished form of mine, endowed with four arms, is established in heaven.
Those who worship the Immeasurable One who has descended to the earth—
O gods, I indeed always dwell within him;
for the gods, turning back, do not attain that state.
Constantly recollecting the Lord with their intellects, the joyful Brahmā and the other lords of the gods, proclaiming His auspicious qualities,
attained their own pure worlds.
16,006.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Dāruka also, having gone to the Kurus and seen the sons of Pṛthā, those great chariot-warriors,
reported that the Vṛṣṇis had been destroyed by one another in the Mausala conflict.
Having heard that the Vārṣṇeyas, along with the Bhojas, Kukuras, and Andhakas, had perished,
the Pāṇḍavas were consumed by grief and became terrified in heart.
Then Arjuna, the beloved friend of Keśava, took leave of them.
He set out to see his maternal uncle and said, "This [city] no longer exists.
O Lord, having gone to the abode of the Vṛṣṇis with Dāruka,
the hero beheld Dvārakā like a woman whose husband has died.

Those women who formerly had a protector in the Lord of the World were then left without a protector; seeing Pārtha as their protector, they cried out. Seeing Arjuna as their protector yet themselves without a protector, they wailed aloud.
The sixteen thousand women were the wives of Vāsudeva;
upon seeing that Arjuna had arrived, a great cry arose from them. But as soon as he saw them, O descendant of Kuru, Arjuna was overwhelmed with tears.
Deprived of Kṛṣṇa and his sons, he was unable to look upon that river of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, which had the horses for its fish, the chariots for its rafts,
the roar of musical instruments and vehicles for its currents, and the houses for its landing-stairs and great crocodiles.

Then the river of Dvārakā appeared, with its clusters of jewel-śaivala plants, garlanded by walls of diamonds, with the waters of its streets as its currents and whirlpools, and its crossroads as its still lakes; it had Rāma and Kṛṣṇa as its great crocodiles.
The wise Arjuna beheld that city, which was like the terrible river Vaitaraṇī gripped by the noose of Time; it was bereft of the bulls of the Vṛṣṇis,
its splendor gone and devoid of joy, like a lotus pond in the winter season.
Having seen that Dvārakā and those wives of Kṛṣṇa, Pārtha,
shedding tears with a cry, fell upon the surface of the earth.
Then, O lord of the people, Satyā the daughter of Satrājit and Rukmiṇī [did the same].
Rushing forward and surrounding Dhanañjaya, they wept aloud. Then, having raised him up and seated him upon a golden throne,
they stood around that high-souled one, attending to him in silence.
Then, having praised Govinda and spoken with him, the Pāṇḍava,
after consoling those women, went to see his maternal uncle.
Vaiśampāyana said:
The bull among the Kurus beheld that high-souled hero Ānakadundubhi lying down, consumed by grief for his sons;
with eyes filled with tears, he— broad-chested and mighty-armed— [approached him].
O Bhārata, Pārtha, even more distressed than the one who was already afflicted, grasped his feet;
and Ānakadundubhi, the mighty-armed slayer of enemies, desired to smell the head of his sister’s son, yet he was unable to do so.
Embracing Arjuna with both arms, the aged and mighty-armed one,
weeping and remembering all his sons, lamented in great distress,
[mourning] for his brothers, sons, grandsons, daughters' sons, and even his friends.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Arjuna, having seen those by whom hundreds of kings and Daityas were conquered, I do not see them here; yet I still live, O Arjuna, for I am difficult to kill."
"O Arjuna, those two disciples of yours who were always dear and highly esteemed—
through their misconduct, O Pārtha, the Vṛṣṇis have met their destruction.
Those two were indeed considered the two preeminent Atirathas among the Vṛṣṇi heroes."
"O Dhananjaya,
O tiger among the Kurus, you and Pradyumna, as well as Yuyudhana and Krishna— whom you always boast about— those two are the very mouth of the Vrishnis' destruction, my dear son."

"But I do not blame Śaineya, nor Hārdikya, O Arjuna, nor Akrūra, nor the son of Rukmiṇī; for the curse alone is the cause here. For the Lord of the World, having displayed his prowess, slew Keśin and Kaṃsa."
He brought the two Videhas under his sway, O Pārtha, as well as the Caidya who was proud of his strength;
he subdued Ekalavya the Naiṣāda, the Kāliṅgas,
the Māgadhas, the Gāndhāras, the King of Kāśī, and the kings of the Maru desert.
Madhusūdana overlooked this misconduct toward the kings of the East, the South, and likewise those of the mountains;
for you, Nārada, and the eternal sages [all know] him.

"Recognize Govinda as the supreme deity, the infallible Acyuta. And that all-pervading Lord Adhokṣaja beheld the destruction of his kinsmen; he, my own son, had constantly looked on with indifference.
O scorcher of enemies, that which was the word of Gāndhārī and of the sages,
the Lord of the world certainly did not wish to make otherwise;
and this, O scorcher of enemies, was witnessed by you as well, your own grandson.
Though he was struck down by Aśvatthāman, he remained alive through that man’s splendor;
yet your friend did not wish to protect these kinsmen of his—
his sons, grandsons, brothers, and even his friends.
Seeing those who had been slain lying there, he then said this to me:
"O bull among men, today the end of this lineage has arrived;
Bībhatsu will come to this city of Dvāravatī."
"The great slaughter of the Vṛṣṇis that has occurred must be told to him.
O Lord, having heard of this misconduct of the Yadus, he who is possessed of great splendor will surely come here quickly; of this I have no doubt."
Know that I am Arjuna, and that Arjuna is indeed I;
just as the individual soul (*jīva*) is the Supreme Brahman according to the certainty of the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*),
understand, O Mādhava, that whatever he may say must be done accordingly.
"Bibhatsu, the son of Pāṇḍu, will attend to your women and children as the time for it arises,
and he will perform the funeral rites for you;
and once Dhananjaya has departed from this city immediately,"
The ocean will submerge this city, complete with its walls and watchtowers.
For I, having undertaken a vow in a certain sacred place,
shall immediately meet my end along with the wise Rāma.
Having spoken thus, Hṛṣīkeśa, whose prowess is inconceivable,
the Lord, left me with the children and departed for some unknown direction.
Thus, I have been reflecting upon those two high-souled brothers of yours.
"Tormented by grief over this terrible slaughter of my kinsmen, I do not eat;
I shall neither eat nor live. By good fortune you have arrived, O Pāṇḍava!
O Pārtha, perform everything in its entirety that was spoken by Kṛṣṇa."
"O Pārtha, having obtained this kingdom, these women, and these jewels, and having been protected by the hero of the Vṛṣṇis and by the Yadus— deprived of them all,
O Phalguna, I shall not be able to look upon the earth."
"O slayer of enemies, I shall indeed renounce these cherished vital breaths.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by his maternal uncle, that Bībhatsu, the scorcher of foes, [replied].
Dejected, he spoke to the dejected Vasudeva:
"O maternal uncle, O Lord, I am not able to remain here for long and behold this earth bereft of the hero of the Vṛṣṇis and the Madhus."
King Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Sahadeva the Pāṇḍava,
Nakula, and Yājñasenī— we six are of one mind.
Furthermore, this time has surely arrived for the king’s departure.
"O best among those who know the proper time, know that this moment has arrived.
O subduer of enemies, I shall take the wives of the Vṛṣṇis, as well as their children and the elderly, and lead them all to Indraprastha."
Having spoken thus to Dāruka, Dhanañjaya addressed these words to him:
"I wish to see the ministers of the Vṛṣṇi heroes without delay.
Having spoken these words, he went to the Sudharmā assembly hall of the Yādavas.
The heroic Arjuna, grieving for the great car-warriors, entered [the hall]. As he sat there upon his throne, all the subjects, as well as the brahmins and the merchants, stood surrounding him.
To all of them— dejected in mind, silent, and dispirited—
Pārtha himself, even more dejected at that time, spoke these words:
"I myself shall lead the people of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas to Śakraprastha."
"The entire city here will be submerged by the ocean.
Prepare your vehicles and various kinds of jewels;
this Vajra shall be your king in Śakraprastha."
"On the seventh day, when the sun has risen clear, we shall all dwell outside; prepare yourselves without delay.
Thus were those citizens addressed by that Pārtha of unwearied deeds.
Then, eager for their own success, they quickly made preparations.
That night, the son of Pṛthā stayed in the residence of Keśava,
suddenly overwhelmed by a great delusion of grief.
Then, when the next day had dawned, the powerful Vasudeva, the descendant of Śūra,
endowed with great splendor, disciplined his mind and attained the supreme goal.
Thereupon, a great sound arose within the residence of Vasudeva.
There was a terrible sound from the women as they cried out and wept; with all their hair disheveled and their ornaments and garlands cast aside,
the women beat their breasts with their hands and lamented piteously.
Devakī, Bhadrā, Rohiṇī, and Madirā—
those foremost of women— resolved to ascend the funeral pyre after their husband.
Then, O Bhārata, [the king] sent Śauri with a large quantity of garlands carried by men.
Then Pārtha had him carried out by a great vehicle;
O bull among men, all the citizens dwelling in Dvārakā, overwhelmed by pain and grief, followed him here and there.
The sacrificial umbrella of his horse-sacrifice and blazing fires preceded that chariot, and the officiating priests likewise went before it;
and those queens, beautifully adorned, followed after that hero.
Surrounded by sixteen thousand women and thousands of young brides,
they prepared that region which had been dear to the great-souled one while he was alive;
having consecrated it for him, they performed the funeral rites for the ancestors.

Then the four wives of that hero, the son of Śūra, who were excellent women, ascended the funeral pyre after him to go to the world of their husband. The son of Pāṇḍu [beheld] him accompanied by those four women.
He caused [the body] to be cremated with sandalwood and various kinds of fragrant perfumes.
Then there arose the sound of the kindled fire,
along with the chanting of the Sāman singers and the wailing of the men.

Then all those Vṛṣṇi heroes and youths, led by Vajra, as well as the women, offered water for the high-souled one. Having thus caused that rite to be performed, Phalguna, whose dharma is never violated, remained steadfast in his duty.
O bull of the Bharata race, he went to where the Vṛṣṇis had perished.
Seeing them fallen in that slaughter, the Kuru prince was deeply afflicted with grief; yet, acting according to the demands of the time, he performed his duty.
Then, according to their importance,
he performed all the funeral rites for those who had been slain by the Brahmanical curse through the clubs produced from *eraka* grass.
Thereupon, having beheld the body of the Blessed One and lamented, the disciple—
Having recalled all those words, which were intensified by delusion and grief,
he then had the bodies of both Rāma and Vāsudeva searched for and cremated by trustworthy men.
O King, the eight principal queens of Kṛṣṇa, headed by Rukmiṇī,
along with the highly fortunate Revatī, entered the fire. As their bodies were embraced by one another, they became cooled by the bliss of that union.
Having performed the funeral rites for them according to the prescribed rules, the Pāṇḍava mounted his chariot on the seventh day and departed in haste,
accompanied by chariots yoked with horses as well as those drawn by oxen, mules, and camels.
Those women of the Vṛṣṇi heroes, weeping and emaciated by grief,
followed the high-souled Dhanañjaya, the son of Pāṇḍu; likewise,
the servants of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, including both cavalrymen and chariot-warriors.
Then, by the command of Pārtha, the citizens and country-folk, surrounding the women— deprived of their heroes and including the old and the young— departed; likewise,
elephant-riders went forth on elephants resembling mountains.
Accompanied by sixteen thousand and eight hundred and thirty-five guards, along with those equipped with superior weapons,
all the sons of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis followed Pārtha,
as did Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of great wealth.
Sixteen thousand women of the inner apartments of Vāsudeva,
placing the grandson of the wise Kṛṣṇa, Vajra, at their head, set forth;
and many thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions [of others] followed as well.
Sixteen thousand, eight hundred and thirty-eight women of the Bhoja, Vṛṣṇi, and Andhaka clans, whose protectors had been slain, went forth.
That vast host of Vṛṣṇis, possessing great power and resembling the ocean itself,
was carried by Pārtha, the best of chariot-warriors and conqueror of enemy cities.
When that people had departed, the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters,
then submerged Dvārakā, which was filled with jewels;
for wherever that tiger among men left the land, [the ocean followed].
That ocean flooded each and every thing with its waters;
and then the ocean spoke to all the living beings there:
"Abandoning your heaps of gold and various kinds of jewels..."
Having abandoned here various vessels made of gold and silver, as well as this most excellent, indestructible substance,
the army, I must now protect this city along with its inhabitants for Hari.

"Furthermore, when my descent shall take place in the Kṛta Yuga, I shall be the treasurer for him; even these [treasures] are not our wealth. Having beheld that marvel, the people dwelling in Dvārakā—
They traveled faster than fast, exclaiming, "Oh, what fate!
And dwelling in delightful forests, on mountains, and by rivers,
Dhanañjaya brought back the wives of the Vṛṣṇis.

Having reached the land of the Five Rivers, which was exceedingly prosperous and rich in cattle, livestock, and grain, the wise lord established his residence there. Then, a greed arose among the bandits who had been deprived of their masters.
O Bhārata, seeing the women being led away by Pārtha alone,
those Ābhīras of evil deeds and ugly appearance, their minds corrupted by greed, gathered together and consulted one another.
"This lone warrior Arjuna, having slain the aged, the children, and those whose lords have been killed, has become arrogant after defeating Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and Jayadratha;
that evil-minded one disregards us as we stand here with staffs in hand."
Passing us by, he leads [the army] away; these warriors here have lost their vigor.
Having slain those led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, and even the Nivātakavacas, and having conquered both Śakra and Rudra, he now disregards us.
Then those thousands of robbers, armed with clubs and carrying stolen goods, rushed toward that multitude of the Vṛṣṇis,
putting the common folk to flight with a great lion-like roar.
Driven by the passage of time, those sixteen thousand and eight, seeking wealth,
rushed forward. Then the son of Kuntī, the mighty-armed Arjuna, having suddenly turned back along with his followers, spoke to them as if laughing:
"Turn back, O you who know not dharma, if you do not wish to die!
Do not now grieve, pierced by arrows and slain by me!
Thus addressed by that hero, they disregarded his words.
Though repeatedly restrained, those deluded people rushed toward the crowd;
then, O Bhārata, Jishnu Arjuna was unable to draw his great, divine, and undecaying bow Gāṇḍīva with all his strength.
He began to string it with great effort, as if by some means;
when the tumultuous confusion arose, he managed to string it with difficulty,
yet it became loose once again.
The arrows discharged by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva did not even pierce his skin;
he reflected upon his celestial weapons, yet he could not recall them. Seeing that great transformation in the battle, as well as [the failure] of the strength of his arms, he was struck with wonder.
He was filled with shame due to the destruction of his great divine weapons;
and all those Vṛṣṇi warriors— whether on elephants, horses, chariots,
or on foot— were unable to turn back that people who were being carried away.
Because his wives were so numerous, as they flocked together from here and there, Pārtha made every effort to protect the people while all the warriors looked on; then those most excellent women—
Sixteen thousand, eight hundred and fifty-seven were dragged away on all sides, while others fled out of fear.
Then the lord Dhanañjaya Pārtha, filled with agitation, struck down the bandits with arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva bow, together with the servants of the Vṛṣṇis.
O King, in an instant those straight-flying arrows of his went to their destruction;
for though they had previously been inexhaustible, those blood-drinking shafts were now spent.
Having encountered this depletion of his arrows, he was struck down by pain and grief.
Then, while Pārtha looked on, the son of Indra (Arjuna) slew those bandits with the tip of his bow;
meanwhile, O Janamejaya, those Mlecchas fled in all directions, carrying away the excellent women of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
But the lord Dhanañjaya reflected in his mind upon that destiny;
overcome by pain and grief, he became intent on sighing.
This was due to the disappearance of his celestial weapons and the exhaustion of the strength of his arms.
Because his bow became uncontrollable and because of the exhaustion of his arrows, Pārtha became despondent, reflecting that "this is destiny. Then,
O King, he turned back and said, "This [power] no longer exists."

Then that high-minded one, taking the remainder of his wife's belongings after most of her jewels had been stolen, descended at Kurukṣetra. Thus, having brought back the remnants of the Vṛṣṇis' wives that had survived the plunder, he arrived.

With Yudhiṣṭhira’s permission, Dhanañjaya, the descendant of Kuru, settled the princes who were the founders of lineages here and there; Pārtha established the son of Hārdikya in the city of Mārtikāvata.

When the Khāṇḍava forest had been burnt, that best of men established him in his kingdom; and the Pāṇḍava then took with him the wives of the Bhoja king who remained after the slaughter, as well as the elderly, the children, and the women.

He settled all those who were bereft of their heroes at Śakraprastha. The righteous-souled one established the beloved son of Sātyaki, Yuyudhānin, along the Sarasvatī, placing the elderly and the children at the forefront.
In Indraprastha, the slayer of enemy heroes gave the kingdom to Vajra; but though restrained by Vajra, Akrūra’s wives departed,
and those of pure heart entered the Sarasvatī, as did others.
Then Rukmiṇī, Gāndhārī, Śaibyā, Haimavatī,
and Queen Jāmbavatī entered the fire;
likewise did Satyabhāmā and the other queens who were dear to Kṛṣṇa.
O King, having resolved upon the life of asceticism, they entered the forest;
subsisting on fruits, roots, and other such foods, and intent solely on meditation upon Hari,
they crossed the Himavat mountains and entered the village of Kalāpa.
As for those men residing in Dvārakā who had followed Pārtha,
Jaya (Arjuna) distributed them among Vajra as was appropriate. Having performed that timely duty, Arjuna was overwhelmed with tears.
16,008.074c O King, he beheld Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana seated in the hermitage.
16,009.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
16,009.001a O King, as Arjuna was entering the hermitage of the truth-speaking sage,
He saw the son of Satyavatī, the sage, seated in a secluded spot. Having approached that knower of dharma who observed great vows, he stood before him;
then, announcing his name, "I am Arjuna," he saluted him.
"Welcome to you," said the sage, the son of Satyavatī;
the great sage, with a serene soul, further said, "Please be seated.
To him, whose mind was troubled and who was sighing again and again—
Seeing Pārtha with a despondent mind, Vyāsa said this:
"Has he been sprinkled with water from a jar by someone whose nails and hair are [disheveled],
while some attendant remains standing right there fast asleep?"
Having fallen from the assembly above, he has gone...
[he who explains the meaning of all the Upaniṣads is the Great Guru].
Having consecrated a Liṅga for him, every single day, one should worship it.
By what has your gift of gold coins, your prostrations, and your religious observances been obstructed?
Day after day, you listen to the Vedānta for two *ghaṭikās*;
have you been struck by dust, or have you killed a Brahmin?
"You appear defeated in battle, like one whose glory has departed.
I do not recognize you; what is this, O bull of the Bharatas?
If it is something I may hear, O Pārtha, you should tell me quickly."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Pārtha, sighing deeply, said, "Listen, O Blessed One," and duly related his own defeat to Vyāsa.
Arjuna said:
"That glorious one of intelligent form, with large lotus-like eyes—
that Kṛṣṇa, together with Rāma, has abandoned his body and gone to heaven."
Recalling that, O Mahāmati, I am always beset by delusion and grief; I am perpetually on the verge of death,
yet the bliss of touching the light of your words is like nectar.
Remembering that high-souled God of gods, I am utterly bewildered—
that Kṛṣṇa, by whose power Bhīṣma, Droṇa, the King of Aṅga, and others such as Duryodhana were consumed, has now abandoned the earth.

The destruction of the Vṛṣṇi heroes at Prabhāsa, brought about by the curse of the Brahmins, occurred in the Mausala age; it was hair-raising and brought an end to those heroes. Those who were the great-souled heroes, possessing the pride of lions and endowed with great strength—
O Brahmin, the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas have slain one another in battle;
those whose arms were like iron clubs and who could withstand maces, bludgeons,
and spears, have now been struck down by blades of *eraka* grass— behold the reversal brought about by Time!

A thousand of those mighty-armed warriors, five hundred in number, have met their destruction, having encountered one another. Again and again, I cannot bear the ruin of those possessed of immeasurable energy.
Reflecting upon the Yadus and the illustrious Kṛṣṇa,
he considered it as impossible as the drying up of the ocean, the moving of a mountain,
the falling of the sky, or the cooling of fire.
"I consider the destruction of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow to be unbelievable;
yet, deprived of Kṛṣṇa, I have no desire to remain here in this world.
O ascetic, hear now of another matter even more painful than this."
My mind is shattered as I think of this again and again,
O Brahmin, seeing my Vṛṣṇi women by the thousands being pursued and carried off in battle by the Ābhīras who dwell in the land of the Five Rivers.
Taking up my bow there, I was unable to string it;
my strength in my two arms was not as it had been before.
O great sage, my various weapons have vanished.
And in an instant, the arrows were exhausted on all sides.
That bow, those weapons, that chariot, and those horses—
all fell away at once, like a gift given to one who is not learned in the Vedas.
And that man of immeasurable self, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace—
four-armed, clad in yellow garments, dark-complexioned, with eyes as broad as lotuses—
he of great splendor goes before my chariot.
Consuming the enemy armies, I do not see him today—
by whose splendor the enemy forces were previously scorched,
and whom I subsequently destroyed with arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Not seeing him, O best of beings, I am despondent and as if reeling; my mind is utterly weary, and I find no peace,
[not seeing] the son of Devakī, the divine Vāsudeva, the unborn Lord.
"Without the hero Janārdana, I have no desire to live.
For as soon as I heard that Viṣṇu had departed, even my very directions became bewildered. My kinsmen and my strength are lost; I am empty and I run about."
"O best of beings, you ought to instruct me for my own welfare.
Vyāsa said:
"Those who were born as portions of the gods from the God of Gods have departed together with him."

"O tiger among the Kurus, the great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas were consumed by the curse of Brahmā and destroyed; they were overlooked by the king for the sake of maintaining and protecting the Dharma. You ought not to grieve for them."
For that must indeed come to pass, as it was ordained for these great-souled ones;
and it was overlooked by Kṛṣṇa, though he was capable of averting it—
for Kṛṣṇa is indeed able to [overthrow] the entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
How much less could he possibly alter the curse of the wise?
Indeed, those women were cursed long ago by the sage Aṣṭāvakra, who was provoked by their jesting; for that reason, there shall be a destruction of your army.
He who goes before the chariot, bearing the discus and the mace,
is the four-armed Vāsudeva, the ancient seer; out of affection for you,
the large-eyed one has brought about the removal of the earth's burden.
Having liberated the entire world, he has gone to his own supreme abode.
But here, O bull among men, O mighty-armed one, you have performed a great deed for the sake of the gods,
with Bhīma as your companion and the twins as well.

"O bull among the Kurus, I consider you to have accomplished your purpose and to be fully perfected; for it is my opinion that the time has come for your departure, as that is what is best. O Bhārata, [you possess] strength, intelligence, splendor, and resolute action."
They arise during times of existence and perish when that state changes.
O Arjuna, kings such as Bhīṣma and Karṇa were previously slain by you alone;
that was not an overcoming by the action arising from Time.
"Because the Kauravas were destroyed by you, and because you were defeated by the Ābhīras—
O Dhanañjaya, all this has Time as its root; Time is the seed of the universe, and it alone takes everything back again according to its own will."
Having been powerful, he becomes weak once again; having been a master here, he is commanded by others once more. And now the weapons, their tasks accomplished, have departed as they came.
"When the time comes, they will return to your hands once more;
O Bhārata, even for you, it is time to go to the supreme destination. For this, O bull of the Bharatas, I consider to be your highest good."
Having understood these words of Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor,
and being granted permission, Pārtha went to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
And having entered the city, the hero approached Yudhiṣṭhira.
He related exactly what had occurred concerning the people of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
